items.stem: A service lift is descending but its downward speed is decreasing. Taking upward as positive, what direction must its net force point?

options.A: Upward, since its acceleration opposes its downward velocity.
options.B: Downward, because it is moving downward.
options.C: Zero, because the slowing is steady.
options.D: The direction cannot be inferred without its mass.

scaffolds.author: NLM-PROD1
scaffolds.text: Name the direction of travel, what happens to speed, and which force quantity is being asked for. Does travel direction alone decide net-force direction?

scaffolds.author: NLM-PROD1
scaffolds.text: Treat a downward velocity as a negative number. Compare an earlier and later velocity when the downward speed is shrinking. Which value is closer to zero, and what does their change per second mean?

scaffolds.author: NLM-PROD1
scaffolds.text: Use the vertical form of Newton's second law, ΣFᵧ = maᵧ. The mass is positive. First infer the acceleration sign from the change in signed velocity, then decide the force direction yourself.

reasoning: The lift moves downward, but its downward speed decreases. Velocity is therefore becoming less negative on an upward-positive axis.
A later velocity minus an earlier velocity is positive, so the acceleration points upward.
By Newton's second law, ΣFᵧ = maᵧ. Because mass is positive, net force is upward.
teacher.check: If the downward speed were constant instead, acceleration and net force would both be zero. Moving down alone does not determine force direction.

feedback.A: Selected A names upward net force. To check your reasoning, compare a later downward velocity with an earlier one: it is less negative, so acceleration is upward and Newton II points net force upward.
feedback.B: Downward is the lift's motion direction, not its acceleration as it slows. With upward positive, its velocity becomes less negative; net force follows acceleration.
feedback.C: A steady rate of slowing still changes velocity. Zero net force would require constant velocity; here it is not constant.
feedback.D: The lift's mass affects the magnitude, not the force direction inferred from the acceleration sign. Newton II ties force direction to acceleration.

items.stem: Two small robots pull against the ends of the same taut strap. Robot A pulls the strap left with 40 N. Which two forces make a Newton-third-law pair at A's connection to the strap?

options.A: Robot A pulls the strap left with 40 N; the strap pulls A right with 40 N.
options.B: Robot B pulls the strap at B's end; the strap pulls B oppositely with equal force.
options.C: Robot A pulls the strap left with 40 N; robot B pulls the strap at B's end.
options.D: The strap pulls A right with 40 N; gravity pulls A downward.

changes: Correct source option A remains at displayed A; its complete reciprocal force detail is restated in parallel two-clause syntax: A-on-strap left 40 N, strap-on-A right 40 N. Previous R1 display C→A; this removes unsupported A→C key rotation.

Displayed B: reciprocal strap–B connection, with opposite equal force but NO invented B force number, direction or equilibrium. B is a real third-law pair at B's DIFFERENT contact, not the requested A–strap contact.
Displayed C: robot A-on-strap (left 40 N) and robot B-on-strap (magnitude unspecified); forces on the SAME strap, hence not a third-law pair.
Displayed D: strap-on-A (right 40 N) and gravity-on-A (downward, magnitude unspecified); forces on the SAME robot A from different interactions.

All display choices are an explicitly authorized adaptation of PHYS-NLM-002; source options A–D, original stem, zero-figure, authored provenance, source key A, source EXPLAIN-D1 remain unchanged in source-rows.v1.json.

reasoning: At the A–strap contact, A exerts a force on the strap and the strap exerts a force on A.
The paired forces act on different objects, have the same magnitude (40 N), and point in opposite directions.
Two forces on the strap, or two forces on A, are not each other's Newton-third-law interaction pair.

feedback.A: This selects the two forces at A's contact. They act on different bodies (strap and A), with opposite directions and equal 40 N magnitudes. Your explanation was recorded but not automatically judged.
feedback.B: This is a reciprocal pair at B's end, not at the requested connection to A. Identify the contact named in the stem; no magnitude for B is given.
feedback.C: Both forces here act on the strap. Third-law partners must act on different bodies at the same interaction.
feedback.D: Both forces act on A, from the strap and gravity. They are not each other's third-law partners.

items.adaptation_defect_note: The source originally has answer-specific rightward 40 N details and shorter distractors; prior R1 C was the unique actor/object reversal and rotated key without a basis. R2 correct A and distractor B are both genuine reciprocal patterns, but only A is at the requested A–strap contact. C/D preserve same-recipient wrong-force pairs; no 40 N asserted for B or gravity. Exact 001 source is not adapted.
